name: Lithium
summary: The gold-standard mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder, uniquely effective for suicide-risk reduction — but with a narrow therapeutic index requiring monitoring.
mechanism: Mechanism not fully understood; modulates inositol signaling and neurotransmitter systems and alters neuronal excitability.

pharmacokinetics.halfLife: ~18–36 h (varies with age and renal function)
pharmacokinetics.onset: Days to 1–2 weeks for acute mania

dosing.adult: 600–1200 mg/day titrated to serum level: 0.8–1.2 mmol/L (acute mania), 0.6–1.0 mmol/L (maintenance)

safety.pregnancy: Teratogenic risk (Ebstein anomaly) with first-trimester exposure; if used, close level and hydration monitoring.
safety.lactation: Enters breast milk (infant levels can be therapeutic) — generally avoided.
contraindications: Significant cardiovascular disease (e.g., sick sinus syndrome)
warnings: Narrow therapeutic index — toxicity above ~1.5 mmol/L
Chronic renal impairment and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with long-term use
NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and thiazides raise lithium levels
monitoring: Serum lithium levels 5–7 days after a dose change, then periodic
Renal function, electrolytes, and hydration status
safety.overdose: Toxicity above ~1.5 mmol/L — tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures; severe toxicity may need hemodialysis.

clinicalPearls: Dehydration is the classic precipitant of toxicity — NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors raise lithium levels.
Check levels 5–7 days after any dose change; target 0.6–1.0 mmol/L for maintenance.
good: Bipolar maintenance and suicide prevention — the gold standard when monitoring is feasible.
bad: Renal disease, dehydration risk, thyroid disease, or patients unlikely to attend level monitoring.

provenance.notes: Curated from standard psychopharmacology references. Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
